## What it is

Gelman's post starts from Matlab's decision to replace its rainbow color map, "jet", with a new default called "parula". Rainbow, he writes, "is well known to be problematic. I'm surprised Matlab stuck with it for so long. I guess the message is that defaults, once set, are hard to change." His second example is R's base graphics, with "tick marks that are too big and axis labels that are too far from the axes": "Everybody has to know by now how bad these defaults are, but nobody changes them."

The same logic reaches beyond graphics, to defaults such as the 0.05 significance threshold, standard table formats and conventional priors. Users have built workflows around a default. Reviewers expect it. Changing it creates incompatibility with past work. So the first default often wins for decades.

## Why it matters

Because defaults are sticky, the moment of *setting* them deserves extra care. A careless default chosen for convenience can shape a field long after its inventor would have changed it. Changing an entrenched default, as with moving away from p < 0.05 or from flat priors in software, takes coordinated effort, because individuals who switch alone pay a cost: their work looks non-standard.

## How it works

A toy model of path dependence. Each period, every user of the old default considers switching. The benefit of switching is the quality gap between the methods *plus* a coordination term that grows with the share of others who have already switched. The cost is a fixed switching cost. Early on, almost nobody has switched, so the coordination benefit is small and few people move. Change is slow at first and then sudden, or it never happens.

## Simulated example

The new method is objectively better. Vary the switching cost and the strength of the coordination effect. Watch how long the old default survives.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof gap = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "Quality advantage of the new method"})
viewof cost = Inputs.range([0, 2], {value: 1.1, step: 0.05, label: "Individual switching cost"})
viewof coord = Inputs.range([0, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Coordination benefit (others switched)"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 39, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
adoption = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const N = 1000;
  let switched = new Array(N).fill(false);
  switched = switched.map(() => r() < 0.02);       // a few early adopters
  const path = [];
  for (let t = 0; t <= 60; t++) {
    const share = switched.filter(Boolean).length / N;
    path.push({t, share});
    switched = switched.map(s => s || (gap + coord * share - cost + r.normal(0, 0.3) > 0 && r() < 0.3));
  }
  return path;
}
```

```{ojs}

})
```

## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# Defaults, once set, are hard to change: adoption with switching costs.
gap <- 0.3 # quality advantage of the new method # <1>
cost <- 1.1 # individual switching cost
coord <- 1 # coordination benefit (grows with the share who switched)
set.seed(39) # <2>

N <- 1000
switched <- runif(N) < 0.02 # a few early adopters # <3>
share <- numeric(61)
for (t in 0:60) {
  share[t + 1] <- mean(switched)
  tempted <- gap + coord * mean(switched) - cost + rnorm(N, 0, 0.3) > 0 # <4>
  switched <- switched | (tempted & runif(N) < 0.3)
}
half <- which(share >= 0.5)[1] - 1 # <5>

if (is.na(half)) {
  cat("Never reaches half adoption within 60 years\n")
} else {
  cat("Half the field switches after", half, "years\n")
}
cat("Final share: ", round(100 * share[61]), "%\n", sep = "")

plot(0:60, share, # <6>
  type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#2166ac", ylim = c(0, 1),
  xlab = "Years after the better method appears",
  ylab = "Share using the new method"
)
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2)
```
1. The page's controls: how much better the new method is, what switching costs an individual, and how much the benefit of switching grows with the share who already have.
2. Fixes the random numbers so the run is reproducible.
3. A few early adopters.
4. Each year, a person is tempted to switch if the quality gap plus the coordination benefit outweighs the switching cost, give or take.
5. When half the field has switched, if ever.
6. Adoption over 60 years. A better method with a high switching cost can stall below the tipping point for decades.

## Python {.unlisted}

```{.python}
# Defaults, once set, are hard to change: adoption with switching costs.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

gap = 0.3   # quality advantage of the new method
cost = 1.1  # individual switching cost
coord = 1   # coordination benefit (grows with the share who switched)
rng = np.random.default_rng(39)

N = 1000
switched = rng.uniform(size=N) < 0.02  # a few early adopters
share = []
for t in range(61):
    share.append(switched.mean())
    tempted = gap + coord * switched.mean() - cost + rng.normal(0, 0.3, N) > 0
    switched = switched | (tempted & (rng.uniform(size=N) < 0.3))
share = np.array(share)
half = np.flatnonzero(share >= 0.5)

if half.size:
    print(f"Half the field switches after {half[0]} years")
else:
    print("Never reaches half adoption within 60 years")
print(f"Final share: {100 * share[-1]:.0f}%")

plt.plot(range(61), share, color="#2166ac", linewidth=2)
plt.axhline(0.5, color="black", linestyle="--")
plt.ylim(0, 1)
plt.xlabel("Years after the better method appears")
plt.ylabel("Share using the new method")
plt.show()
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Defaults persist through coordination and switching costs, not because they are good.
- Take special care when *setting* a default. You may be choosing for a generation.
- Changing an entrenched default needs coordinated, institutional action, not just individual persuasion.
:::
